AO.CARD.001.short: Follow the Introit while the priest completes the quiet opening prayers. You do not need to keep pace with the silent text.
AO.CARD.001.long:
What is happening
The Mass begins while two things can happen at once. The schola sings the Introit, the Proper entrance chant of the day, while the priest completes the preparatory prayers at the foot of the altar and approaches the altar. These are parallel parts of the same liturgical opening, so the priest may be several prayers ahead of or behind the chant.

What should I do?
Stand for the entrance. While the Introit is being sung, follow the chant or listen prayerfully; you do not need to race through the priest’s quiet opening prayers. Follow the local congregation for the precise moment of kneeling or sitting.

Why this matters
The entrance chant gives the liturgical day its first public voice, while the priest’s quiet preparatory prayers dispose him to approach the altar. For the faithful, the public chant is therefore the natural common act of worship; the private priestly preparation can be understood without being treated as a text everyone must follow.

How this developed
Before 1960
Before the 1960 reform, the Roman Mass already had the entrance chant alongside the priest’s prayers at the foot of the altar and ascent prayers. In solemn celebrations, several priestly recitations ran in parallel with what the choir or sacred ministers were doing.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 Code simplified a number of duplications in sung Mass, but the 1962 Missal still retains the Prayers at the Foot, Aufer a nobis, Oramus te and the priest’s own altar-side sequence. The Introit remains the public sung entrance text.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the postconciliar Roman Missal, the Prayers at the Foot and the private ascent prayers disappeared from the Order of Mass. The Entrance Chant remains, but the priest goes to the chair after reverencing/incensing the altar and begins the Sign of the Cross, greeting and Penitential Act as public Introductory Rites.

Why the difference matters
This explains why a 1962 Sung Mass has two simultaneous clocks at the beginning: the congregation can legitimately be following the Introit while the priest is still completing quiet preparatory prayers.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public chant. At the altar: Foot prayers → ascent → altar. The schola: Introit. The next reliable landmark is Kyrie.

Priest and schola
Introit is the public liturgical clock while the priest’s preparatory prayers are quiet.

For prayer
Ask for the grace to enter the Sacrifice deliberately: leave distraction behind and let the chant of the day give your prayer its first orientation.

Sources

AO.CARD.002.short: Follow the sung Kyrie to its final invocation. The priest and Schola may finish at slightly different times.
AO.CARD.002.long:
What is happening
The Kyrie is the Church’s repeated plea for mercy. At Sung Mass the priest and schola each complete the Kyrie according to the rite, and their timing does not have to coincide exactly.

What should I do?
Join the Kyrie if you are singing the responses; otherwise listen and pray the invocation attentively. Stay with the sung Kyrie until its final invocation.

Why this matters
The Kyrie is both acclamation and supplication: the Church addresses the Lord and asks for mercy. Its repetitive form is not filler; it gathers the assembly into a common plea before the principal oration.

How this developed
Before 1960
The traditional Roman Kyrie developed as a ninefold litany: Kyrie three times, Christe three times, Kyrie three times.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 Code explicitly retains the ninefold Kyrie in the 1962 regime.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal normally repeats each acclamation twice, although more repetitions remain possible for musical or linguistic reasons. The Kyrie is normally a congregational/choir acclamation and may form part of the Penitential Act.

Why the difference matters
The number and function of the invocations changed. A user coming from the current Roman Rite may otherwise expect a sixfold Kyrie and advance too early.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public chant. At the altar: At altar · Kyrie. The schola: Kyrie. The next reliable landmark is Gloria if appointed; otherwise Collect.

Priest and schola
Stay with the sung Kyrie until its final invocation.

For prayer
Place your sins and needs before Christ without anxiety: ‘Lord, have mercy’ is already a complete prayer.

AO.CARD.003.short: After the priest intones the Gloria, follow the words actually sung by the schola (choir). Return to the priest when the public Gloria ends.
AO.CARD.003.long:
What is happening
The priest intones the Gloria and the schola continues the hymn. In the 1962 Sung Mass the priest also recites the Gloria at the altar, so he may finish before the singing does and may sit while the schola continues.

What should I do?
Follow the words actually being sung. Stand while singing; if the local ceremonial has the congregation sit when the ministers sit, follow that custom. Make any phrase-linked bows or signs at the sung words, not when the priest privately reaches them.

Why this matters
The Gloria is the Church’s great hymn of praise to the Father and to Christ the Lamb. Its movement from adoration and thanksgiving to petition makes it more than a festive song: it is a compact confession of who God is and what the Church asks from him.

How this developed
Before 1960
In the older sung Roman practice, the celebrant intoned and recited the Gloria while the choir continued the sung text, so priest and choir could be at different textual points.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
That parallelism remains in 1962: after the intonation, the celebrant recites the Gloria and may sit while the Schola continues.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal treats the Gloria as one public hymn: it is sung by everyone together, by people and choir alternately, or by the choir alone; if recited, it is recited communally rather than by a separate priestly track.

Why the difference matters
This is why the 1962 app should follow the words actually being sung for congregational bows and gestures rather than the priest’s private progress.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public sung text while also watching the priest’s visible action. At the altar: Private recitation / choir continues. The schola: Gloria. The next reliable landmark is Collect after the public Gloria ends.

Priest and schola
After the priest’s intonation, the choir carries the public Gloria; return to Priest at the final Amen.

For prayer
Join the praise of the angels and the Church; notice how the hymn moves from God’s glory to the Lamb who takes away sin.

AO.CARD.004.short: Stand and listen to the Collect. Answer Amen when the public prayer is complete.
AO.CARD.004.long:
What is happening
The priest gathers the prayer of the Church in the Collect. This is a public presidential prayer: the people listen and ratify it with Amen.

What should I do?
Stand, listen to the Collect and answer Amen. Let the prayer itself, rather than the priest’s earlier private pace, control the card.

Why this matters
The Collect ‘collects’ the prayer of the Church into the priest’s presidential prayer and expresses the character of the day. The faithful make it their own by the Amen.

How this developed
Before 1960
Earlier Roman Missals often accumulated commemorations and additional orations, so a Collect could be followed by further collects for occurring or commemorated observances.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1955 and especially 1960 reforms sharply reduced the older system of multiple orations and commemorations. The 1962 Missal is already a simplified stage compared with earlier twentieth-century practice.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal normally has one Collect. It also contains a substantially revised and enlarged corpus of presidential prayers and permits choices in defined circumstances.

Why the difference matters
The Collect is a good example of continuity of function with major simplification of the older calendar-and-commemoration machinery.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: Epistle side · chanting Collect. The next reliable landmark is Epistle / Lesson.

Priest and schola
The Collect is a public priestly prayer.

For prayer
Put one concrete intention into the Church’s prayer, then make the final Amen your own.

AO.CARD.005.short: Sit and listen to the Epistle or Lesson. When it ends, the schola (choir) takes over with the chants before the Gospel.
AO.CARD.005.long:
What is happening
The Epistle or Lesson is proclaimed publicly. In the reformed 1960–1962 sung rite, the public proclamation is the reading the congregation should follow; it is not merely background to a second private reading by the celebrant.

What should I do?
Sit and listen to the Lesson or Epistle. At the end, remain with the public liturgy as the schola begins the chant before the Gospel.

Why this matters
The reading is not background information but proclamation of God’s word to the Church. The faithful’s task is principally to listen and receive rather than to track the celebrant’s private actions.

How this developed
Before 1960
At Solemn Mass the Epistle belonged to the subdeacon, while the celebrant also read liturgical texts at the altar; older practice contained more duplication between celebrant and ministers.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 reform removed important duplications in sung Mass: when a sacred minister or lector proclaims a reading, the celebrant is no longer required to duplicate it privately in the same way.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Rite, proclamation of the non-Gospel readings is normally ministerial rather than presidential and may be entrusted to instituted or other suitable readers. Sundays and solemnities normally have three readings, using the postconciliar multi-year lectionary.

Why the difference matters
The 1962 public reading should be treated as the congregation’s real liturgical event, not as a cue to chase a simultaneous private priestly reading.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: Epistle side · proclaiming Epistle. The next reliable landmark is Gradual and the interlection chants.

Priest and schola
At the end of the Epistle, the interlection chants become the public clock.

For prayer
Listen for one word, command, promise or warning that God is placing before the Church today.

AO.CARD.006.short: Remain with the Gradual and Alleluia, Tract or Sequence. The priest may already be preparing for the Gospel while the chant continues.
AO.CARD.006.long:
What is happening
The Gradual and the Alleluia, Tract or Sequence form the sung meditation between the readings. They can last much longer than the priest’s immediate preparations, so the priest may already be moving or preparing for the Gospel while the schola is still singing.

What should I do?
Remain seated unless your local sung practice directs otherwise. Listen to or sing the Gradual and Alleluia, Tract or Sequence; do not switch merely because the priest has already begun preparing for the Gospel.

Why this matters
The chants between the readings prolong and meditate on the Word just heard and prepare the assembly for the Gospel. In the 1962 sung rite they are themselves liturgical action, not musical interludes while something more important happens elsewhere.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Roman Gradual, Alleluia, Tract and prescribed Sequences formed the chant between the readings; their length could create a substantial interval while ministers prepared for the Gospel.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains this Proper-chant structure. The 1960 reform changes surrounding rubrical mechanics but does not turn the Gradual into a responsorial psalm.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The postconciliar Roman Missal restored the Responsorial Psalm as the normal chant after the first reading and reorganized the acclamation before the Gospel. The traditional Gradual and Tract remain possible in the Graduale Romanum, but the ordinary parish structure is different.

Why the difference matters
This is one of the clearest places where a person formed by the current Roman Rite can misread the 1962 timeline: a long chant is not a delay but the actual public liturgical action.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public chant. At the altar: Waiting / preparing for Gospel. The schola: Gradual · Alleluia / Tract / Sequence. The next reliable landmark is Public Gospel announcement.

Priest and schola
When the chant complex ends, the public Gospel becomes the next clock.

For prayer
Do not rush toward the Gospel. Let the chant create a space in which the Word already heard can descend from the ear into the heart.

AO.CARD.007.short: Stand for the public Gospel. Make the customary three small crosses at the announcement, then listen to the proclamation.
AO.CARD.007.long:
What is happening
The Gospel is proclaimed publicly with greater solemnity than the other readings. The announcement, the customary small crosses, the standing posture and the proclamation itself all direct attention to Christ speaking in the Gospel.

What should I do?
Stand. At the Gospel announcement make the customary small crosses on forehead, lips and breast if that custom is being followed, then listen to the proclamation.

Why this matters
The Gospel is given special honor because Christ speaks to his people in the Gospel proclamation. Standing, the acclamations, incense and the small crosses all express attentive reception of his word.

How this developed
Before 1960
The solemn Gospel had its own ministerial procession, incense and chant, while the celebrant could also have a separate reading track at the altar.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 reform removes the need for the celebrant to duplicate the Gospel when it is sung by the proper minister. The 1962 public Gospel therefore becomes an especially strong common clock.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Rite likewise treats the Gospel as the high point of the Liturgy of the Word, proclaimed by the deacon or priest from the ambo. The people stand and make the three small crosses at the Gospel announcement.

Why the difference matters
This is a point of strong continuity: the public Gospel, not any private preparatory prayer, is the event the congregation should follow.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible words and visible action. At the altar: Gospel side · proclamation. The schola: Responses. The next reliable landmark is Sermon if present; otherwise Credo or Offertory.

Priest and schola
The public Gospel controls.

For prayer
Make the three small crosses consciously: may Christ’s Gospel be in your mind, on your lips and in your heart.

AO.CARD.008.short: Sit and listen to the sermon. Wait for the liturgical action to resume before advancing the Mass timeline.
AO.CARD.008.long:
What is happening
The sermon or homily is a period of instruction connected with the liturgical readings and Christian doctrine. Its length does not tell you where the hidden liturgical action has reached; wait for the public rite to resume.

What should I do?
Sit and listen. Do not advance the Mass timeline because of elapsed time; wait until the celebrant resumes the liturgical action.

Why this matters
The sermon explains the faith and applies the proclaimed Word to Christian life. During it the correct participation is receptive attention, not continued navigation through hidden ritual steps.

How this developed
Before 1960
A sermon could be preached in connection with Mass, but in the older rubrical conception it was not integrated into the Order of Mass in the same way as the postconciliar homily.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
In 1962 the sermon remains a real pastoral and instructional moment but is not one of the priest’s liturgical prayer texts in the Ordo Missae.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
Sacrosanctum Concilium gave the homily a stronger liturgical status, and the current Roman Missal treats it as part of the Liturgy of the Word; on Sundays and holy days with the people it is ordinarily required.

Why the difference matters
The app should pause liturgical navigation during the sermon rather than infer hidden progress, while also explaining that its formal status differs between the 1962 and current books.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: Preaching place · homily. The next reliable landmark is Credo if appointed; otherwise Offertory.

Priest and schola
Follow the preacher; Mass resumes only when the liturgical action resumes.

For prayer
Listen for the truth you are being asked not merely to understand but to live after Mass.

AO.CARD.009.short: After the priest intones Credo, follow the sung Creed. Let the public sung text—not the priest’s private pace—control the gesture at Et incarnatus est.
AO.CARD.009.long:
What is happening
The priest intones Credo and the schola continues the Creed. As with the Gloria, the priest’s own recitation can move at a different pace from the singing, so the congregation’s gestures should follow the words actually being sung.

What should I do?
Follow the Creed as it is sung. Stand while singing; follow the local practice if the ministers sit during a long setting. At Et incarnatus est make the gesture required by the day and your posture: normally a genuflection when standing, a bow when already seated, with the special kneeling rule on Christmas and the Annunciation.

Why this matters
The Creed is the Church’s public response of faith to the Word proclaimed. It gathers the principal mysteries of faith immediately before the Eucharistic Sacrifice, so the bodily reverence at the Incarnation belongs to the actual public confession being sung.

How this developed
Before 1960
In sung Roman practice the celebrant recited the Creed while the choir continued it, producing the same kind of parallel clock seen in the Gloria.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 regime retains that parallelism. The public sung words govern the congregation’s timing, including the Incarnatus gesture.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Missal the Creed is sung or said by the priest together with the people. The bodily gesture also changed: a profound bow is now normal at Et incarnatus est, with genuflection on the Nativity and Annunciation.

Why the difference matters
The difference matters directly to live guidance: in 1962 the Schola’s sung text can control the faithful’s gesture even when the celebrant has already passed the phrase.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public sung text while also watching the priest’s visible action. At the altar: Private recitation / choir continues. The schola: Credo. The next reliable landmark is Offertory.

Priest and schola
After the priest’s intonation, follow the public sung Creed; return after Amen.

For prayer
At Et incarnatus est, adore the humility of the Son of God who took flesh for your salvation.

AO.CARD.010.short: Follow the Offertory chant while it sounds. When it ends, the visible preparation at the altar becomes the better guide.
AO.CARD.010.long:
What is happening
The Offertory begins after Oremus. The schola sings the Offertory chant while the priest prepares and offers the bread and wine and, where used, incense is offered. The chant and the altar action therefore overlap.

What should I do?
Sit after Oremus according to the usual 1962-era congregational practice. Follow the Offertory chant while it sounds; when the chant ends, let the visible action at the altar become your main landmark.

Why this matters
The Offertory prepares the bread and wine for the Eucharistic Sacrifice and invites the faithful to unite their own self-offering to Christ’s offering. The quiet priestly prayers explain and prepare the gifts; the chant gives the congregation a common public act during that preparation.

How this developed
Before 1960
The traditional Offertory developed a rich set of priestly prayers over the bread and wine, with the Offertory antiphon sung in parallel at High Mass.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the traditional Offertory prayers, Lavabo and incensation. Much of this remains quiet or ministerial while the Schola sings.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The postconciliar reform substantially simplified the Preparation of the Gifts. The bread and wine may be brought by the faithful; the priest says the revised offering formulas, usually quietly, while an Offertory chant may accompany the action.

Why the difference matters
The theological purpose—preparing the gifts for the Eucharistic Sacrifice—continues, but the visible and textual architecture changed considerably after the Council.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Offertory prayers at altar. The schola: Offertory. The next reliable landmark is Orate fratres.

Priest and schola
Follow the Offertory chant while sounding; when it ends, the altar action becomes the better landmark.

For prayer
Place your work, duties, sufferings and intentions spiritually with the gifts being prepared, asking that your life be united to Christ’s offering.

AO.CARD.011.short: Attend to Orate fratres and the response. During the silent Secret, remain recollected and wait for the public Preface dialogue.
AO.CARD.011.long:
What is happening
The priest turns and asks the faithful to pray that the sacrifice may be acceptable to God. After the response he says the Secret quietly. The next strong public landmark is the audible conclusion leading into the Preface.

What should I do?
Attend to Orate fratres and make the response where your participation mode provides it. During the Secret remain recollected; you may read it in the missal, but wait for the audible Preface dialogue as the next reliable public cue.

Why this matters
Orate fratres makes explicit that priest and faithful are united in offering the Sacrifice, though in different ways according to their state. The Secret asks God to receive and sanctify the offerings and leads directly into the Eucharistic thanksgiving.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Orate fratres led into the Secret, whose name reflects its quiet recitation. Earlier Masses could have several Secrets corresponding to multiple Collects.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the silent Secret, but the 1960 simplification reduces the older multiplication of orations.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The Secret becomes the Prayer over the Offerings and is proclaimed aloud as a presidential prayer; there is normally one, and the people answer Amen. Orate fratres remains.

Why the difference matters
A modern user may expect an audible prayer immediately after Orate fratres. In 1962 the silence is itself normal and the Preface dialogue is the next strong public cue.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible words and visible action. At the altar: Orate fratres → Secret. The schola: Offertory may continue. The next reliable landmark is The public Per omnia / Preface dialogue.

Priest and schola
Orate fratres is public; the Secret is quiet but the priest remains the useful clock.

For prayer
When the priest says Orate fratres, consciously consent to the offering of the Sacrifice; during the Secret, place yourself silently before God.

AO.CARD.012.short: Stand and follow the Preface dialogue and Preface. When the Preface ends, the Sanctus begins.
AO.CARD.012.long:
What is happening
The Preface is a public dialogue and solemn prayer of thanksgiving leading directly to the Sanctus. It is one of the clearest points at which priest and congregation are again on the same audible timeline.

What should I do?
Stand and make the dialogue responses. Listen to the Preface and remain with the priest’s public voice until the Sanctus begins.

Why this matters
The Preface is the Church’s solemn act of thanksgiving before the Canon. ‘Lift up your hearts’ is not merely a dialogue cue: it tells the faithful what interior posture the Eucharistic Prayer requires.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Preface dialogue and Preface were already public/sung and formed the audible gateway into the Canon.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The same structure remains in 1962. The Preface is one of the strongest synchronization points because it is public and leads directly to the Sanctus.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal retains the same basic dialogue and Preface function but provides a much larger collection of Prefaces and connects them to several Eucharistic Prayers.

Why the difference matters
This is a major continuity point across forms: when the Preface begins, private drift collapses back into a common public clock.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: At altar · Preface. The next reliable landmark is Sanctus.

Priest and schola
At the end of the Preface, the Sanctus begins.

For prayer
At Sursum corda, deliberately lift the heart away from distraction and toward thanksgiving.

AO.CARD.013.short: Follow the Sanctus and Benedictus while they are actually sung. The priest may already have entered the silent Canon.
AO.CARD.013.long:
What is happening
The Sanctus is sung while the priest begins the Canon. In Gregorian practice the Sanctus and Benedictus form one chant; in the 1958 discipline governing non-Gregorian settings, the Benedictus may follow the Consecration. The priest’s silent Canon can therefore continue underneath the music.

What should I do?
Sing or listen to the Sanctus. Kneel according to the local 1962 practice as the Canon begins. If the Benedictus continues or resumes later, follow the chant without assuming the priest has stopped the Canon.

Why this matters
In the Sanctus the earthly Church joins the worship of the angels and acclaims the holiness and glory of God. It is the threshold between the Preface and the Canon and therefore one of the strongest spiritual and navigational landmarks of the Mass.

How this developed
Before 1960
Sanctus and Benedictus were part of the Ordinary, but polyphonic practice often created a practical split around the Consecration.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1958 instruction distinguishes the Gregorian case, where Sanctus-Benedictus may be sung continuously, from non-Gregorian settings in which singing must cease for the Consecration and the Benedictus may follow afterward.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal treats the Sanctus, including Benedictus, as a single acclamation of the whole assembly within the Eucharistic Prayer. It is not structured as a separate post-Consecration continuation.

Why the difference matters
This is crucial for Ad Orientem because the Schola may still be singing while the priest has entered the Canon in 1962; the current rite usually does not create the same textual drift.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Entering the Canon. The schola: Sanctus · Benedictus. The next reliable landmark is Canon / sacred silence.

Priest and schola
Follow Sanctus/Benedictus while sung; when the choir falls silent, the Canon may be followed on the priest track.

For prayer
Join the worship of heaven: the holiness you acclaim is the holiness before which the Sacrifice is about to be offered.

AO.CARD.014.short: The Canon is being prayed quietly. Remain recollected; following its text is optional. The warning bell and elevations are the next major landmarks.
AO.CARD.014.long:
What is happening
The Canon, the central Eucharistic prayer of the 1962 Mass, is now prayed quietly at the altar. The congregation is not required to keep word-for-word pace with the priest. Sacred silence, the priest’s visible actions and the approaching Consecration are the important landmarks.

What should I do?
Kneel and remain recollected. You may follow the Canon in the missal, but you are not required to keep exact pace with the silent text. Watch for the warning bell and the priest’s visible preparation for the Consecration.

Why this matters
The Canon is the heart of the Eucharistic Sacrifice: thanksgiving, consecration, offering, remembrance and intercession are gathered into the priestly prayer. The faithful participate by faith, adoration, self-offering and interior union; they are not required to read every secret word.

How this developed
Before 1960
For many centuries the Roman Canon was the single Eucharistic Prayer of the Roman Mass and was prayed in a low voice after the Sanctus.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the Roman Canon as the sole Canon, largely secret except for specified audible moments.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The postconciliar Missal retained the Roman Canon as Eucharistic Prayer I but added other Eucharistic Prayers. The Eucharistic Prayer is proclaimed audibly, while the people participate by attentive silence and prescribed acclamations.

Why the difference matters
The long silent Canon is not an accidental gap in 1962; it is a defining structural difference from the current Roman Rite and must be explained rather than filled with forced navigation.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Silent Canon. The schola: Silence. The next reliable landmark is Warning bell → Consecration of the Sacred Host.

Priest and schola
The Canon is secret; following the text is optional. Warning bell/elevations override both tracks.

For prayer
During the silent Canon, you may adore, offer yourself, remember the living and dead, or simply remain attentive before God. Silence is itself a legitimate participation.

AO.CARD.015.short: Give full attention to the altar. Remain kneeling; at the elevation of the Host, bow reverently and then look upon the Sacred Host.
AO.CARD.015.long:
What is happening
At the words of Consecration over the bread, the bread becomes the Body of Christ. The priest genuflects and elevates the Sacred Host for the adoration of the faithful. This sacramental action takes priority over every other track.

What should I do?
Remain kneeling. At the elevation, bow reverently and then look upon the Sacred Host in adoration. Do not let any chant or secondary text distract from the elevation.

Why this matters
At the Consecration of the Host, Christ becomes sacramentally present under the species of bread by the words and action of Christ spoken through the priest. The elevation is ordered to adoration; the faithful’s attention should therefore converge on the Sacred Host.

How this developed
Before 1960
The elevation of the consecrated Host and the accompanying genuflections had long become major visual moments of Western Eucharistic devotion; bells developed as an audible signal.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the quiet words of Consecration, genuflection, elevation and prescribed bell signals. The faithful’s attention naturally converges on the visible elevation.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal retains the showing/elevation of the Host and the priest’s genuflection. Bells remain optional according to circumstances and local custom. The words of institution are proclaimed audibly and are followed by the memorial acclamation.

Why the difference matters
The elevation is a hard visual override in both forms, but in 1962 it carries even more navigational weight because the surrounding Canon is silent.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Consecration of the Sacred Host. The schola: Sacred silence. The next reliable landmark is Consecration of the Chalice.

Priest and schola
The elevation is the decisive visual/sacramental landmark.

For prayer
At the elevation of the Host, look upon Christ with faith and make a simple act of adoration, love or reparation.

AO.CARD.016.short: Remain kneeling and attend to the Chalice. Bow reverently and look upon It when it is elevated.
AO.CARD.016.long:
What is happening
At the words of Consecration over the wine, the wine becomes the Precious Blood of Christ. The priest genuflects and elevates the Chalice for the adoration of the faithful.

What should I do?
Remain kneeling. At the elevation, bow reverently and look upon the Chalice in adoration.

Why this matters
At the Consecration of the Chalice, the Precious Blood becomes sacramentally present under the species of wine. The separate consecrations sacramentally represent the Sacrifice of Christ, and the elevation calls forth adoration.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Chalice elevation developed in parallel with the Host elevation as a principal moment of Eucharistic adoration.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the quiet Consecration of the Chalice, genuflection, elevation and bell signal.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal retains the Chalice elevation and genuflection. Bells may accompany it by local custom, and the memorial acclamation follows the Consecration.

Why the difference matters
As with the Host, the visible elevation is a more reliable congregational landmark than trying to hear the priest’s low voice.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Consecration of the Chalice. The schola: Sacred silence. The next reliable landmark is Post-Consecration Canon.

Priest and schola
The elevation is the decisive visual/sacramental landmark.

For prayer
At the elevation of the Chalice, adore the Precious Blood poured out for the remission of sins and entrust to Christ those most in need of mercy.

AO.CARD.017.short: The Canon continues quietly. If the Benedictus resumes, follow the schola (choir); otherwise remain in sacred silence until the Canon’s public conclusion.
AO.CARD.017.long:
What is happening
The Canon continues quietly after the Consecration. The Church prays for the living and the dead and moves toward the final doxology. If a delayed Benedictus is being sung, it may sound during this part of the Canon.

What should I do?
Remain kneeling and continue in adoration and prayer. If the Benedictus is sung after the Consecration, follow it as the public chant; otherwise remain in sacred silence until the Canon’s public conclusion.

Why this matters
After the Consecration the Canon remembers Christ’s saving mysteries, offers the holy Victim to the Father, prays for the living and dead, and asks that those who receive may be filled with grace. Sacred silence allows the faithful to unite themselves to these intentions without needing word-for-word synchronization.

How this developed
Before 1960
After the elevations the Roman Canon continued quietly through the anamnesis, oblation, intercessions and prayers for the dead.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
That long silent continuation remains in 1962, with only particular phrases becoming audible.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Missal the Eucharistic Prayer continues aloud. A memorial acclamation by the people is inserted after the Consecration, and the prayer proceeds audibly through anamnesis, oblation and intercessions.

Why the difference matters
The 1962 faithful may legitimately remain in sacred silence or use a missal without needing to synchronize every sentence; the current rite gives the assembly a more audible common track.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Canon after the Consecration. The schola: Benedictus may resume. The next reliable landmark is Canon doxology / minor elevation.

Priest and schola
If Benedictus resumes, follow it; otherwise remain in sacred silence / priest Canon.

For prayer
Remember the living and the dead for whom you want this Sacrifice offered, and unite your own life to the offering on the altar.

AO.CARD.018.short: Watch for the minor elevation and the audible Per omnia saecula saeculorum. The silent Canon is ending and the Pater noster follows.
AO.CARD.018.long:
What is happening
The priest concludes the Canon with the doxology and the minor elevation of the Host and Chalice. The audible Per omnia saecula saeculorum and Amen bring the silent Canon to a public conclusion and lead into the Pater noster.

What should I do?
Watch the minor elevation. When Per omnia saecula saeculorum is heard, make the response and prepare to follow the Pater noster.

Why this matters
The doxology brings the Canon to its climax by giving all glory to the Father through Christ, with Christ and in Christ. The elevation of the Sacred Species and the Amen mark the public completion of the Eucharistic Prayer.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Canon concluded with the doxology Per ipsum and a small elevation of Host and Chalice, distinct from the major elevations at the Consecration.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains this minor elevation and the audible conclusion leading to the response Amen.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal gives the concluding doxology a very prominent public role: the priest elevates paten and chalice while proclaiming the doxology, and the people answer the Great Amen.

Why the difference matters
The minor elevation is the clearest sign that the silent Canon is ending; it should be used as a strong synchronization point.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Canon conclusion · minor elevation. The schola: Silence. The next reliable landmark is Pater noster.

Priest and schola
Minor elevation and public Per omnia reset the common timeline.

For prayer
Let the final Amen be a real assent: all glory is offered to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

AO.CARD.019.short: Follow the Pater noster and make the response when it comes. This is the public beginning of the Communion rite.
AO.CARD.019.long:
What is happening
The priest chants or recites the Pater noster. In the 1962 Roman Mass the celebrant normally says the prayer, while the people or server make the concluding response Et libera nos a malo.

What should I do?
Stand according to the usual sung-Mass practice and follow the Pater noster. Make the prescribed response at its conclusion; do not assume the whole congregation recites the entire prayer in every 1962 form.

Why this matters
The Lord’s Prayer begins the immediate preparation for Communion. Its petitions for daily bread, forgiveness and deliverance are especially fitting as the faithful approach the Eucharistic Bread.

How this developed
Before 1960
In the older Roman Mass the priest recited or sang the Pater noster; the congregation’s ordinary liturgical response was concentrated at its conclusion, although twentieth-century Dialogue Mass permissions allowed broader recitation at Low Mass.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Sung Mass still preserves the priest-led Pater noster as a distinct public priestly chant, with the response at the end.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Missal the priest and all the faithful say or sing the Lord’s Prayer together; the priest then says the embolism and the people conclude with the doxology For the kingdom.

Why the difference matters
The text is the same Lord’s Prayer, but the actor assignment changed substantially; the app must not import current congregational recitation into a 1962 Sung Mass.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: Pater noster. The schola: Pater noster. The next reliable landmark is Libera nos · Fraction · Pax Domini.

Priest and schola
Pater noster is public.

For prayer
Pray the Lord’s Prayer as immediate Eucharistic preparation, especially the petitions for daily bread, forgiveness and deliverance.

AO.CARD.020.short: Follow the visible Fraction and the public Pax Domini. The Agnus Dei follows.
AO.CARD.020.long:
What is happening
The priest continues with Libera nos, breaks the Sacred Host and gives the public Pax Domini. The Fraction is a strong visible landmark when the prayer itself is quiet.

What should I do?
Use the visible Fraction as your landmark during the quiet Libera nos. When Pax Domini is heard, follow the public response and prepare for the Agnus Dei.

Why this matters
The Fraction recalls Christ’s breaking of the bread and prepares the Sacred Species for Communion; the commixture expresses the unity of Christ living and glorious. The prayer for peace asks that Communion bear its ecclesial fruit of unity.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Libera nos, Fraction, commixture and Pax formed a tightly connected priestly sequence. In Solemn Mass the Pax could be transmitted hierarchically among clergy rather than exchanged generally by the congregation.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 rite retains that structure: the Pax Domini is public, but the actual Pax is a ministerial ceremonial in Solemn Mass, not a general congregational handshake.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal places an optional Sign of Peace for the faithful before the Fraction. The Agnus Dei accompanies the Fraction, and the manner of exchanging peace is regulated by episcopal conferences.

Why the difference matters
This is a major behavioral difference. A user formed by the current rite should not be prompted to exchange peace with neighboring faithful during the 1962 Mass.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Libera nos · Fraction · Pax. The next reliable landmark is Agnus Dei.

Priest and schola
After Pax Domini the Agnus becomes the public sung clock.

For prayer
Ask that Christ heal divisions and make you an instrument of the peace that flows from communion with him.

AO.CARD.021.short: Follow the sung Agnus Dei. When it ends, prepare quietly for Holy Communion.
AO.CARD.021.long:
What is happening
The Agnus Dei accompanies the breaking and preparation for Communion. Its repeated invocation turns the congregation from the completed Canon toward peace, mercy and preparation to receive the Lamb of God.

What should I do?
Follow the Agnus Dei. After it ends, kneel and prepare inwardly for Holy Communion.

Why this matters
The Agnus Dei addresses Christ as the sacrificial Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Its petitions for mercy and peace move the faithful from the completed Sacrifice toward sacramental reception.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Agnus Dei had a fixed threefold form in the Roman Mass, with the third invocation ending dona nobis pacem outside Requiem.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the three invocations and the Requiem textual variant.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal links the Agnus Dei directly to the Fraction and allows repetition as often as necessary until the Fraction is complete, with the final invocation ending grant us peace.

Why the difference matters
The current rite uses the chant functionally to cover the Fraction; the 1962 app should not wait for an indefinite number of repetitions.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public chant. At the altar: Agnus Dei / Communion preparation. The schola: Agnus Dei. The next reliable landmark is Prayers before Communion.

Priest and schola
After Agnus, private Communion preparation follows.

For prayer
Repeat the petitions inwardly: mercy for sin, peace in the soul, peace in the Church and peace among those you must forgive.

AO.CARD.022.short: The priest is saying his private prayers before Communion. You may follow them, but your own preparation for Communion is primary.
AO.CARD.022.long:
What is happening
The priest now says his private prayers before receiving Communion. These prayers belong to his immediate preparation; the faithful may follow them in a missal, but they are not a compulsory word-for-word congregational track.

What should I do?
Remain kneeling and prepare yourself for Communion. If you wish, open the priest’s private prayers as a secondary text; do not treat them as something the congregation must recite.

Why this matters
The priest’s private prayers before Communion ask for peace, deliverance from sin and worthy reception. Their existence teaches that even the celebrant prepares personally for Communion; the faithful should make their own preparation rather than merely observe his.

How this developed
Before 1960
After the Agnus Dei the priest had a group of private prayers preparing for Communion, including the prayer for peace and two personal preparation prayers.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains these private priestly prayers. They are not congregational texts and do not create a public timing obligation.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The prayer for peace is said aloud before the Sign of Peace, while immediately before Communion the priest quietly chooses one of two personal preparation prayers.

Why the difference matters
This is precisely the kind of silent priestly material that belongs in the optional deep rubric rather than as the congregation’s compulsory main card.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Prayers before Communion. The schola: Agnus may finish. The next reliable landmark is Communion of the Priest.

Priest and schola
Priest’s private prayers may be followed, but interior preparation is primary.

For prayer
Make your own preparation for Communion: faith, humility, contrition, desire and love are more important than keeping pace with the priest’s private text.

AO.CARD.023.short: The priest now receives Holy Communion. Remain recollected and wait for the public Communion invitation before treating the faithful’s Communion as begun.
AO.CARD.023.long:
What is happening
The priest receives the Sacred Host and Precious Blood. If the faithful will receive Communion, the public invitation to them follows after the priest’s own Communion.

What should I do?
Remain kneeling and prepare for Communion. The priest’s own reception is the main visible landmark; wait for Ecce Agnus Dei before treating the Communion of the faithful as begun.

Why this matters
The celebrant receives the Sacrament before distributing Communion to the faithful. His Communion belongs to the integrity of the Eucharistic celebration, while the faithful are invited to complete their participation sacramentally when properly disposed.

How this developed
Before 1960
The priest’s Communion preceded Communion of the faithful, and the priest’s own Domine non sum dignus belonged to his preparation.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
In 1962 the priest receives the Host and Precious Blood before the separate public invitation to the faithful. Older bell customs at the priest’s Domine non sum dignus were curtailed when the faithful were to communicate.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Missal the priest and people make one common act of humility at the Ecce Agnus Dei; the priest then receives Communion and the Communion chant begins immediately as he receives.

Why the difference matters
The priest’s Communion is not yet the faithful’s Communion invitation in 1962. The app must not advance the user to their own reception too early.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Communion of the Priest. The next reliable landmark is Ecce Agnus Dei, if the faithful receive.

Priest and schola
Visible Communion of the priest is the landmark.

For prayer
As the priest receives, renew your desire to receive Christ worthily and ask for the grace of a fruitful Communion.

AO.CARD.024.short: Attend to Ecce Agnus Dei and the three Domine non sum dignus. When distribution begins, the Communion chant becomes the useful public text/chant.
AO.CARD.024.long:
What is happening
The priest shows the Sacred Host and says Ecce Agnus Dei. In the strict 1962 books the older second Confiteor before the people’s Communion is omitted; the faithful then make the threefold Domine non sum dignus before distribution.

What should I do?
Look toward the Sacred Host at Ecce Agnus Dei. If you will receive, make the three Domine non sum dignus with the congregation and prepare to approach. If your church retains an older second Confiteor by custom, recognize it as a local survival rather than the strict 1962 sequence.

Why this matters
Ecce Agnus Dei directs everyone’s attention to Christ truly present and the Domine non sum dignus expresses the humility and faith of the centurion. This is the immediate spiritual threshold of the faithful’s Communion.

How this developed
Before 1960
Before the 1960 reform, a second Confiteor before Communion of the faithful was widely embedded in the ritual sequence.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960/1962 reform suppresses that second Confiteor as part of the Communion rite. The Ecce Agnus Dei is followed by the threefold Domine non sum dignus for Communion of the faithful.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal has no second Confiteor here. Priest and people say Lord, I am not worthy once together after Behold the Lamb of God.

Why the difference matters
This is an important reform boundary because many traditional communities retained the older second Confiteor by custom even though it is not part of the strict 1962 books.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible words and visible action. At the altar: Ecce Agnus Dei / faithful preparation. The next reliable landmark is Distribution of Holy Communion.

Priest and schola
Once distribution begins, the Communion chant is useful while waiting.

For prayer
Look toward the Host and make the centurion’s words your own: humility does not keep you away from Christ; it prepares you to receive him.

AO.CARD.025.short: While waiting, follow the Communion chant and distribution. When your own turn comes, stop following the text/chants and receive Holy Communion.
AO.CARD.025.long:
What is happening
Holy Communion is distributed to the faithful. The Communion chant accompanies the public distribution, but when your own turn comes your personal act of receiving Christ takes priority over following either priest or schola.

What should I do?
If you are waiting to receive, follow the Communion chant or pray quietly. When your turn comes, stop following the timeline and give full attention to receiving Holy Communion. After receiving, return to your place and make your thanksgiving.

Why this matters
Holy Communion unites the communicant sacramentally to Christ offered in the Sacrifice and deepens the unity of his Mystical Body. At the moment of reception, personal sacramental action takes priority over every navigation track.

How this developed
Before 1960
The older Roman manner of Communion ordinarily had the faithful kneel at the rail and receive the Host on the tongue from the priest, with the longer distribution formula and no communicant Amen.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
That remains the normative 1962 ceremonial profile: the priest gives Communion under the species of bread with the traditional formula while the communicant receives.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal uses The Body of Christ with the communicant answering Amen. Episcopal norms govern posture; Communion may be received on the tongue and, where permitted, in the hand, and Communion under both kinds is possible in defined circumstances.

Why the difference matters
This is not a cosmetic difference: the communicant’s words, posture and reception mechanics are different enough that the app must branch by rite rather than reuse modern Communion instructions.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Distributing Holy Communion. The schola: Communion. The next reliable landmark is Priest returns to altar / ablutions.

Priest and schola
Your own Communion turn overrides both tracks; otherwise follow Communion chant/distribution.

For prayer
When your turn comes, stop reading. Approach, adore and receive. The sacramental encounter is now the whole point.

AO.CARD.026.short: Remain in thanksgiving. Follow the Communion chant while it continues; when distribution and chant end, the priest’s ablutions become the clearer landmark.
AO.CARD.026.long:
What is happening
After Communion the priest purifies the sacred vessels while the Communion chant may still be continuing or coming to an end. For someone who has received Communion, personal thanksgiving is now more important than tracking every ablution prayer.

What should I do?
If you have received Communion, remain in thanksgiving. If you have not, continue prayerfully while distribution ends. Sitting after Communion can be permitted by local practice; follow the congregation where the custom is clear.

Why this matters
The ablutions reverently ensure that the Sacred Species are consumed and the vessels purified; the Communion chant and subsequent silence support thanksgiving. The faithful should turn from anticipation to gratitude for the gift received.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Communion antiphon and the priest’s ablutions followed the Communion sequence, with chant timing shaped by whether and how long the faithful communicated.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1958 discipline specifies that when the faithful communicate at sung Mass the Communion chant begins with the actual distribution, not simply with the priest’s private Communion.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal begins the Communion chant while the priest receives and prolongs it through the people’s Communion. Purification may occur at the altar, credence table or after Mass according to the rubrics.

Why the difference matters
The start trigger of the Communion chant changed. That difference directly affects which track should control the Ad Orientem card.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Ablutions / Communion antiphon. The schola: Communion may continue. The next reliable landmark is Postcommunion.

Priest and schola
Stay with Communion chant while it sounds; switch when chant/distribution end and ablutions dominate.

For prayer
After receiving, give thanks before asking for anything else. If you did not receive, make a spiritual communion and remain united to the Sacrifice.

AO.CARD.027.short: Stand for the Postcommunion and answer Amen. The common public timeline has resumed.
AO.CARD.027.long:
What is happening
The priest returns to the missal and says the Postcommunion, the public prayer after Communion. The congregation is again on a common audible timeline and answers Amen.

What should I do?
Stand, listen to the Postcommunion and answer Amen. In penitential or Requiem contexts the local posture can differ, so follow the form being celebrated.

Why this matters
The Postcommunion is the Church’s official prayer for the fruits of the Sacrament just received. It gathers personal thanksgiving into the public prayer of the Church.

How this developed
Before 1960
Earlier Roman Masses could have multiple Postcommunions corresponding to multiple Collects and Secrets.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1955/1960 simplifications greatly reduce that older multiplication, though the 1962 calendar can still produce more than one oration in defined cases.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal has a single Prayer after Communion, normally preceded by a period of sacred silence after distribution.

Why the difference matters
The function remains thanksgiving and petition for the fruits of the mystery, but the surrounding structure is simpler in the current rite.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible public prayer. At the altar: Postcommunion. The next reliable landmark is Dismissal.

Priest and schola
Postcommunion is public.

For prayer
Ask that what you have received at the altar become visible in your conduct after Mass.

AO.CARD.028.short: Follow the dismissal and make the response. Do not assume every Mass has the same ending: the blessing and Last Gospel depend on the form.
AO.CARD.028.long:
What is happening
The priest gives the dismissal appropriate to the Mass. Some forms and special celebrations have a different conclusion, so the app must follow the actual rite rather than assume Ite, missa est in every case.

What should I do?
Stand and make the response to the dismissal. Remain attentive because the blessing or Last Gospel may be omitted or altered in some special forms.

Why this matters
The dismissal sends the faithful from the sacred action back into Christian life. The Mass is not an escape from duty: grace received in worship is ordered to faithful action, witness and charity.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Roman conclusion used several formulas according to the day and rite, including Ite, missa est, Benedicamus Domino and Requiescant in pace.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 reform narrows and reorganizes when these formulas occur, but the 1962 Missal still preserves different conclusions for ordinary Mass, certain liturgical continuations and Requiem.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal provides several dismissal formulas centered on sending the people forth; Benedicamus Domino and Requiescant in pace no longer function as the ordinary branching system of the 1962 Mass.

Why the difference matters
The dismissal is not merely a fixed phrase in 1962; it can tell the user what kind of ending follows.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Dismissal. The schola: Dismissal response. The next reliable landmark is Placeat / Final Blessing.

Priest and schola
Dismissal is public; Schola/people give the response.

For prayer
Receive the dismissal as a command: carry what has been offered and received into work, family, charity and duty.

AO.CARD.029.short: Remain attentive during the quiet Placeat. When the priest turns to bless the people, kneel and make the customary Sign of the Cross where that blessing is given.
AO.CARD.029.long:
What is happening
The priest says the Placeat quietly and, where the rite provides it, turns to give the final blessing. The blessing is a distinct public action even though the Placeat immediately before it is private.

What should I do?
Kneel for the blessing where it is given and make the customary Sign of the Cross. In forms without the ordinary blessing, follow the rite shown by the app.

Why this matters
The final blessing asks God’s grace upon the faithful as they return to ordinary life. In 1962 the quiet Placeat immediately before it also expresses the priest’s humble petition that the Sacrifice be acceptable.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Placeat was a quiet priestly prayer before the final blessing, and the blessing itself was omitted in certain Masses.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1962 Missal retains the quiet Placeat and the traditional blessing pattern, with defined exceptions such as Requiem and cases ending with Benedicamus Domino.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The Placeat is no longer part of the Order of Mass. The concluding rites instead move from greeting to blessing—simple, solemn, or Prayer over the People—and then dismissal.

Why the difference matters
A person used to the current rite may think the silence after the dismissal is dead time. In 1962 it can contain the Placeat before the priest turns for the blessing.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the public liturgical action. At the altar: Placeat → final blessing. The next reliable landmark is Last Gospel.

Priest and schola
Quiet Placeat leads into the visible final blessing.

For prayer
Receive the blessing as grace for the concrete obligations awaiting you outside the church.

AO.CARD.030.short: Stand for the Last Gospel and genuflect at Et Verbum caro factum est. Remain until the Gospel has actually concluded.
AO.CARD.030.long:
What is happening
The priest goes to the Gospel side and reads the Last Gospel, normally the Prologue of St John. The congregation stands and genuflects at Et Verbum caro factum est before the Gospel concludes.

What should I do?
Stand for the Last Gospel. Make the customary three small crosses at the announcement if used locally, and genuflect at Et Verbum caro factum est. Rise and remain until the Gospel has ended.

Why this matters
The Prologue of St John places the mystery of the Incarnation at the threshold between the altar and the return to the world: the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us. In the 1962 rite it is also a real liturgical conclusion with its own required gesture at Et Verbum caro factum est.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Last Gospel became a regular conclusion of the Roman Mass, and before 1960 the rubrics also contained a broader system of proper Last Gospels on certain days.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
The 1960 reform suppresses most proper Last Gospels. The 1962 Missal normally retains John 1:1–14 as the Last Gospel, with specified omissions and exceptions.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The postconciliar Order of Mass removes the Last Gospel entirely. The Mass concludes with blessing, dismissal, veneration of the altar and departure.

Why the difference matters
This is one of the clearest visible differences between 1962 and the current Roman Rite. The app must not treat the dismissal or blessing as the end when a Last Gospel still follows.

What should I follow now?
For orientation, follow the priest’s audible words and visible action. At the altar: Last Gospel. The next reliable landmark is Mass complete → After-Mass lifecycle.

Priest and schola
Last Gospel is the public final text unless omitted by a special branch.

For prayer
At ‘the Word was made flesh,’ adore the Incarnation and ask to carry Christ into the world you are about to re-enter.

PRE.ASPERGES.short: This is a pre-Mass sprinkling rite. Stand, follow the chant, and sign yourself when actually sprinkled; the final Amen ends the rite and hands to the Introit.
PRE.ASPERGES.long:
What is happening
The 1962 Roman Missal The 1962 Ritus appendix directly gives the Sunday Asperges/Vidi aquam ceremony: the celebrant sprinkles clergy and people while the prescribed antiphon and psalm are sung/said, with seasonal modifications, then returns below the altar steps for the concluding versicles and prayer.

What should I do?
This is a pre-Mass sprinkling rite. Stand, follow the chant, and sign yourself when actually sprinkled; the final Amen ends the rite and hands to the Introit. Stand; sign when sprinkled. Asperges when applicable; actor/form scope explicit.

Why this matters
The sprinkling recalls baptismal cleansing and disposes the faithful for the Sacrifice that is about to begin. In 1962 it remains a distinct pre-Mass rite, so its final Amen is a genuine structural boundary.

How this developed
Before 1960
The Sunday sprinkling with Asperges me, or Vidi aquam in Paschaltide, was a distinct rite before the principal Mass rather than part of the Mass itself.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
That boundary remains explicit in the 1962 usage: the sprinkling rite ends with its concluding collect and Amen; only then does the Mass begin. Palm Sunday is an exception because its own palm rite replaces the ordinary Sunday sprinkling.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
In the current Roman Missal a blessing and sprinkling of water may replace the Penitential Act on Sundays, especially in Easter Time. It therefore functions inside the Introductory Rites rather than as the same pre-Mass Asperges structure.

Why the difference matters
This historical change is essential for app navigation: in 1962 the final Amen is a hard handoff from a pre-Mass rite to the Mass; in the current rite the sprinkling can itself occupy the place of the Penitential Act.

Priest and schola
Follow the public chant/sprinkling. Final Amen → Mass / Introit.

For prayer
Receive the sprinkling as a reminder of baptism and ask for purity of heart before Mass begins.

Sources
Roman Missal (1962) / proper special-rite books; 1960 Code of Rubrics; current General Instruction of the Roman Missal 51

POST.MASS.short: The liturgical action has ended. Do not treat the priest’s departure as a cue to abandon thanksgiving; remain for a suitable time of prayer according to your circumstances.
POST.MASS.long:
What is happening
The 1962 Roman Missal After the Last Gospel and the prescribed reverence, the celebrant receives the biretta, covers his head and returns to the sacristy with the minister preceding him as on the way in, saying the Benedicite antiphon or other prayers. After removing the vestments he continues thanksgiving for a suitable period.

What should I do?
The liturgical action has ended. Do not treat the priest’s departure as a cue to abandon thanksgiving; remain for a suitable time of prayer according to your circumstances. Remain standing for departure; thanksgiving separate. Outside core Mass chronology.

Why this matters
The Eucharistic Sacrifice bears fruit beyond the final liturgical formula. Personal thanksgiving allows the communicant to remain consciously united to Christ and to carry the grace of the Mass into ordinary duty.

How this developed
Before 1960
Extended private thanksgiving after Mass was strongly encouraged in traditional Catholic spiritual practice and was never reducible to the final liturgical formula.

In the 1960–1962 reform state
Pope Pius XII explicitly taught that personal thanksgiving after Mass remains fitting and should not be abandoned merely because the liturgical celebration has ended.

After the Council / in the current Roman Rite
The current Roman Missal builds a period of sacred silence after Communion into the Mass itself, while personal prayer after Mass remains a legitimate devotional continuation rather than another liturgical section.

Why the difference matters
The app should distinguish the end of the liturgy from the end of personal prayer: the user can leave the Mass timeline while still being invited to thanksgiving.

Priest and schola
No track switch; this is post-Mass thanksgiving.

For prayer
Remain for a suitable time in thanksgiving, adoration and petition according to your circumstances.

Sources
Pope Pius XII, Mediator Dei (1947); current General Instruction of the Roman Missal 88
